opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think there are a few different levers, and the one I find most compelling is what people sometimes call a "race to the top." The idea is that if you can show safety practices are compatible with being a frontier lab, with building useful products, staying competitive, and doing good research, you take away one of the main excuses for not doing them. A lot of the resistance to safety measures comes from a worry that they'll slow you down or cost you commercially. If you can show that's not necessarily true, or that the cost is manageable, it gets much easier for other companies to adopt them.

The Responsible Scaling Policy is a good example. The core idea is to commit in advance: as models get more capable, here are the safety and security measures we'll need in place before we keep training or deploying. Once one lab publishes something like that and shows it can actually operate under it, it becomes a template. Other labs can look at it, critique it, and adopt their own versions. Since then we've seen other companies put out frameworks that are similar in spirit. They're not identical, and I have opinions about which parts are stronger or weaker, but the conversation has moved from "should we have something like this?" to "what should be in it?" That's real progress.

Another lever is publishing safety research. Interpretability work, alignment techniques, red-teaming methods, evaluations for dangerous capabilities: if those stay internal, they only help one lab. If you publish them, other labs can use them, and it raises the baseline for the whole field. There's some tension here, because you don't want to publish things that mainly advance capabilities, but a lot of safety work is clearly net positive to share.

There's also a policy angle. Voluntary commitments from individual companies are a good start, but they're fragile. If competitive pressure gets intense enough, a company could walk back what it committed to. So part of the hope is that by figuring out what workable safety practices look like, you give governments something concrete to build regulation on. It's much easier for a policymaker to say "everyone should do roughly this" when several companies are already doing it and it clearly isn't crippling them.

And then there's a talent dynamic that's easy to underrate. A lot of people working in AI care about safety. If one lab is visibly taking it seriously, that affects where people want to work, and it creates pressure inside other companies, because their own employees ask, "Why aren't we doing this?"

I'd add one caveat. None of this works if you're not actually at the frontier. If you're far behind, nobody has to listen to you, and you can't credibly claim that safety is compatible with competitiveness. So there's an uncomfortable tension: to have influence, you have to build very capable models, which is part of the thing you're worried about. I think that tradeoff is worth it right now, but it's something we have to keep re-examining honestly instead of treating it as settled.

r001.rationale: It says an RSP can serve as a template for other labs and that showing safety measures are compatible with competitiveness can reduce resistance and encourage adoption.

r002.rationale: It says workable practices can give governments a basis for regulation and policymakers can require similar practices when companies show they are feasible.

r003.rationale: It identifies publishing safety research and methods as a way for other labs to use them, raising the field’s baseline.

r004.rationale: It says a lab visibly prioritizing safety while operating at the frontier can demonstrate compatibility with competitiveness and influence other companies.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think there are a few different mechanisms here, and it's worth separating them out.

The first one is just demonstrating that it's possible. A lot of the pushback you hear on safety practices is some version of "that sounds nice, but it would slow us down too much" or "that's not actually workable at the frontier." And the most convincing counterargument to that isn't a blog post, it's existing. If Anthropic can be at the frontier and have a Responsible Scaling Policy, and run red-teaming and evaluations before deployment, and not fall hopelessly behind, that removes the excuse. It shifts the conversation from "is this feasible" to "why aren't you doing it." I think that's probably the most important lever, honestly, and it's also the hardest, because it requires us to actually stay competitive.

The second is being really concrete and public about what we're doing. When we published the RSP, we didn't do that primarily because we needed a public document to hold ourselves to it. We did it partly so other labs could look at it, criticize it, copy the parts that made sense, and improve on the parts that didn't. And you did see something like that: OpenAI put out their Preparedness Framework, DeepMind put out their Frontier Safety Framework. They're not identical, and I'm sure they'd say they got there independently, which is probably partly true. But I think having a fairly detailed worked example out there makes it much easier for someone inside another company to go to their leadership and say, "Look, here's what this actually looks like, we should have one of these."

The third is the research itself. A lot of what the alignment and interpretability teams publish is just free to use. If someone finds a better technique for detecting a model behaving deceptively, every lab can adopt it. We're not trying to keep a moat on safety research. That's kind of the point.

And then the last piece, which I think people sometimes underrate, is policy. There's a limit to how far voluntary commitments get you. If it's a race, and some companies are willing to cut corners, then eventually the ones who aren't cutting corners are at a disadvantage. So part of the strategy has to be supporting regulation that sets a floor everyone has to meet. Then it's not "Anthropic encouraging others," it's just the rules. I think the healthiest outcome is that the stuff we do voluntarily today is eventually just required, and the frontier of what counts as "good safety practice" moves past it.

I'd also be honest that there's a tension in all of this. The whole premise of Anthropic is a bet that it's better to have safety-focused labs at the frontier than to cede that ground. But being at the frontier does contribute to the race dynamics we're worried about. I don't think there's a clean resolution to that. You just try to make the bet pay off: make the safety work good enough and visible enough that it actually pulls the field toward it, rather than just being one more competitor.

r001.rationale: The response says a public RSP can serve as a concrete example for other labs to copy and discuss, but does not state that adopting RSP-like policies gives companies incentives to improve safety.

r002.rationale: It says regulation sets a safety floor so companies that cut corners cannot gain an advantage, making mitigations required across the industry.

r003.rationale: It says Anthropic’s published alignment and interpretability research is free to use and that every lab can adopt useful techniques.

r004.rationale: It argues that operating at the frontier while using safety practices demonstrates their feasibility and can pull other labs toward them.

astra-6.text:
I think the biggest thing is to make good safety practices concrete and show that they’re workable. It’s easy to say companies should take safety seriously. It’s much more useful to demonstrate a way to evaluate a model for dangerous capabilities, explain what you’ll do if you find them, and show that you can actually follow through on those commitments.

Then other companies have something they can adopt or improve on. And ideally, you share enough of the underlying research that they don’t have to recreate everything themselves. We should want safety work to spread across the industry.

There’s also an important role for setting expectations. If one company makes credible commitments and is transparent about how it meets them, that gives employees, customers, and policymakers a basis for asking other companies to do the same.

But I wouldn’t want to rely entirely on voluntary commitments or on everyone following our example. Competitive pressures are real. So part of the goal should be to help establish sensible standards that apply across frontier developers, including us.

r001.rationale: The response mentions credible commitments and standards, but does not state that adopting RSP-like policies would create incentives for companies to improve safety.

r002.rationale: It calls for sensible standards across frontier developers, but does not mention regulation requiring safety mitigations or the incentives such regulation would create.

r003.rationale: It proposes sharing enough of the underlying safety research so other companies can adopt or improve the practices without recreating the work.

r004.rationale: The response says one company’s credible commitments can give others a basis for being asked to act, but does not clearly propose Anthropic demonstrating this by operating a frontier lab that prioritizes safety.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the most useful thing we can do is make good safety practices concrete and show that they’re workable. It’s much easier for another company to adopt a practice if there’s a clear example of what it involves, how you evaluate whether it’s working, and what you do when the results are concerning.

So that means sharing evaluation methods, being candid about limitations, and making commitments that actually affect deployment decisions. If a safety policy never changes what you’re willing to release, it’s hard to know how much substance it has.

But I wouldn’t want this to depend entirely on other companies voluntarily following our example. There are competitive pressures that make that difficult. We should also support common standards and external accountability, so that taking sensible precautions becomes an expectation across the industry.

r001.rationale: The response does not mention RSP-like policies or say that adopting them would incentivize companies to improve safety.

r002.rationale: It calls for common standards and external accountability, but does not state that regulations requiring safety mitigations would incentivize improvement.

r003.rationale: It proposes sharing evaluation methods, but does not identify publishing Anthropic’s safety research as a way to help others reproduce its practices.

r004.rationale: It refers generally to showing workable practices and following an example, but does not identify Anthropic’s operation of a safety-prioritizing frontier lab as that example.
